first.rationale: The two live symptoms (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) point at the funnel, and the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue rather than raw acquisition. Triage therefore targets the two inherited beliefs that are simultaneously most decision-consequential and most weakly evidenced against that objective. memory_86 is the direct basis for my intended action, yet its stated outcomes stop at completion rate, time-to-value, and 'early adoption' — all proximal metrics with no observed link to retention or revenue; shortening onboarding can plausibly buy completion by stripping qualification, data capture, and setup depth, which would raise a funnel metric while lowering downstream account value. memory_73 is the strongest competing pull (the competitor's entry pricing makes discounting the emotionally obvious response) and it is the belief most likely to be misleading here: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is exactly the pattern that can mask discount-attracted, price-elastic, high-churn cohorts, and matching a competitor's price floor is structurally hard to unwind. Verifying it is worth a slot even though I do not currently intend to act on it, because if the source record shows durable qualified revenue it would genuinely change the ranking, and if it shows only short-horizon acquisition it retires a recurring temptation. I did not spend budget on memory_57 (it already carries an explicit retention-neutrality claim, so it is better supported on the durability dimension), on memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist does not address the SMB-side declines driving this quarter), or on memory_91 (in-product activation messaging is a reasonable fallback but a narrower lever than the onboarding path, and it does not touch the completion drop). Standing intent is simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale with a holdout, but instrumented so the primary read is downstream qualified revenue and 30/60-day retention, not completion rate alone; if the memory_86 record turns out to be completion-only with no downstream measurement, I will keep the same direction but tighten to a guarded test and treat the inherited lift as unconfirmed rather than established. Uncertainty is preserved: none of these memories are discarded, and the verification outcomes update confidence rather than settle the question.

final.rationale: Both verifications paid off and they resolve in opposite directions. exp_86 came back stronger than the summary implied: the shortened onboarding flow lifted completion +13% and cut time-to-value by 2.1 days, but critically it also moved 30-day retention +3%. That is the downstream link I was worried was missing — the completion gain was not bought by stripping setup depth or qualification, since accounts that went through the shorter flow survived better, not worse. My main objection to acting on memory_86 is therefore retired, and it now supports the objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue) rather than just a proximal funnel metric. exp_73 confirmed the failure mode I flagged: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% look excellent in isolation, but 30-day retention fell 12% and the source record explicitly states the discounted cohort does not survive the first renewal cycle, with a direct instruction not to generalize targeted discounting as a sustainable-growth strategy. So the competitor's aggressive entry pricing must not be answered with promotional_pricing this week — matching a price floor would import exactly that churn-loaded cohort and would be structurally hard to unwind. The consolidated memory_73 was misleading by omission, and I am treating the archived record as authoritative over it. Given a single non-carryover slot, simplify_onboarding is the right use: it is the only candidate that directly addresses both live symptoms (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%, which are causally linked through time-to-value) and is now the only candidate with verified retention-positive evidence. It is also the correct competitive response — beating the competitor on time-to-value rather than on price defends the price-insensitive part of the base instead of buying the price-sensitive part. Runners-up: activation_messaging (memory_91) remains a plausible fallback but is unverified and narrower, touching engagement without addressing the completion drop; referral_incentive (memory_57) does not address either declining metric; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is off-target for SMB-side declines. Scale is standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout: exp_86 is one prior study under different conditions, and the current quarter's declines may have a cause the earlier test did not face, so I want a holdout and a real read rather than assuming transfer. Uncertainty preserved: primary metric remains downstream qualified revenue and 30/60-day retention, not completion rate, so that the known failure pattern from exp_73 would be caught if it recurs here; memory_73 is not deleted but re-scoped to short-horizon acquisition only.
